name: CRDTs
intent: Data structures that every replica can update independently, even offline, and that always converge to the same value when replicas exchange state, with no coordination.
scenario: A post's like counter and tag set are replicated in three regions. A network partition separates them; each region keeps taking likes, unlikes, tag adds and tag removes. When the partition heals the replicas merge in whatever order messages arrive, with duplicates, and must all end up identical without losing anyone's update.
problem: Replicas that accept writes independently will diverge, and the usual fixes cost availability or data: a single leader or a quorum refuses writes during a partition, while 'last write wins' silently discards concurrent writes and trusts clocks that skew. Plain sets have no good merge at all: if one replica removed an element while another added it, which wins? Without a principled merge rule, offline-first apps, multi-region counters and collaborative editors lose data or need a coordinator.

howItWorks.title: Design the state as a join-semilattice
howItWorks.text: A state-based CRDT (CvRDT) has states that form a partial order and a merge that returns the least upper bound of two states. That merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent: merge(a,b) = merge(b,a), merge(a,merge(b,c)) = merge(merge(a,b),c), merge(a,a) = a. Updates must also move the state upward in the order. Those four properties are the whole proof that replicas converge, whatever the delivery order, and with duplicates.

howItWorks.title: Counters: one slot per replica
howItWorks.text: A G-Counter is a vector with one integer per replica. A replica only increments its own slot; merge is the element-wise max; the value is the sum. A PN-Counter is two G-Counters, P for increments and N for decrements, value = sum(P) - sum(N). The state is O(replicas) however many updates happen, and a replica never overwrites another's slot, so no increment can be lost.

howItWorks.title: Sets: unique tags make remove safe
howItWorks.text: A G-Set only grows (merge = union). A 2P-Set adds a tombstone set, but a removed element can never be re-added. An OR-Set (observed-remove) tags every add with a unique id, such as (replica id, counter). Remove deletes only the tags it has observed, by recording them as tombstones. A concurrent add carries a tag the remover never saw, so it survives: add wins, and add-after-remove works. Merge is the union of the add set and the union of the tombstones.

howItWorks.title: Registers: say what happens to concurrent writes
howItWorks.text: A last-writer-wins register keeps (value, timestamp) and merges by the larger timestamp, with the replica id as a tie-break. It converges, but it discards one of two concurrent writes and its winner depends on wall clocks, so a replica with a clock 5 seconds fast can overwrite newer data. A multi-value register (Riak siblings, Dynamo's shopping cart) keeps all concurrent values, tagged with version vectors, and hands the conflict to the application.

howItWorks.title: Operation-based variant and delivery
howItWorks.text: An operation-based CRDT (CmRDT) ships operations instead of state. It is cheaper on the wire, but it needs reliable broadcast with causal delivery (each operation delivered exactly once, after everything it depends on), or concurrent operations must commute. State-based CRDTs only need an eventually-connected gossip, which is why anti-entropy with Merkle trees and delta-state CRDTs, which ship only the recent changes, are the practical middle ground.

howItWorks.title: Sequences, metadata and garbage
howItWorks.text: Collaborative text uses sequence CRDTs (RGA, Logoot, Yjs, Automerge) that give every character a unique, ordered identifier so concurrent inserts interleave deterministically. The price is metadata: tombstones and identifiers can outweigh the visible text, and they can only be discarded once every replica is known to have seen the delete (causal stability), which needs membership knowledge and some coordination.

pros: Writes are always accepted locally, even offline or during a partition: no coordinator and no quorum on the write path
Convergence is a mathematical property of merge, not of the network: any order and any duplicates give the same result
No lost updates for counters and sets, unlike last-write-wins
Fits offline-first apps, multi-region active-active databases and peer-to-peer sync, where a leader is unavailable or too far away
cons: Only eventual consistency: reads can be stale and two replicas can show different values until they merge
Cannot enforce global invariants (balance >= 0, unique usernames, stock never below zero): each replica checks only its own view
Metadata grows: per-replica vectors, unique tags and tombstones, and sequence identifiers; garbage collection needs causal-stability knowledge
Semantics can surprise users: add-wins sets resurrect an element a user just deleted; merging text can interleave edits in odd ways
Hard to design correctly; the data type's merge, not the application code, has to carry the proof
whenToUse: Counters, presence, likes, flags and sets that must stay writable on every replica, in multiple regions or offline
Offline-first and local-first apps and collaborative editing, where users must keep working without a connection and merge later
Active-active multi-region stores where cross-region round trips on every write are unacceptable (Redis Enterprise Active-Active, Riak data types)
Data where the application can accept 'merge both sides' semantics, for example a shopping cart where a removed item may reappear
whenNotToUse: Anything with an invariant across replicas: account balances, inventory that must not oversell, unique constraints, seat booking. Use a leader, a quorum, consensus or a reservation scheme instead
When one region can safely own the write path and a simple leader gives you strong consistency at acceptable latency
Last-writer-wins data that really is a single value overwritten by the latest write, where a plain timestamped register is enough and its clock risk is acceptable
High-churn data with large tombstone or identifier overhead and no way to coordinate garbage collection
pitfalls: Using last-write-wins for a counter or a set: it converges, but it silently throws away concurrent updates, and clock skew chooses the winner
Letting a replica write another replica's slot or reuse a replica id (cloned VM, restored backup): two writers on one slot make max-merge lose increments
Assuming 'no coordination' means 'no cleanup': OR-Set tombstones and sequence identifiers grow forever unless a garbage-collection protocol runs
Checking 'balance >= 0' locally on each replica and expecting it to hold after the merge: three replicas each pass the check and the merged value goes negative
Using an operation-based CRDT over a transport that duplicates or reorders messages, without causal delivery and de-duplication
Forgetting that remove only affects observed adds: a delete that races an add is lost by design (add wins), which users may read as a bug

roles.label: Replica
roles.description: A full copy of the data that accepts reads and writes locally and merges state received from other replicas.

roles.label: Network
roles.description: The link between replicas, which can partition, delay, duplicate and reorder messages.
